summary: Okanogan County peak 7,154 ft: a wooden L-4 tower built 1935, gone by 1952. A hiker's undated trip report describes summit benchmarks and small remnants.

facts.design: Wooden tower with an L-4 cab. The register and FireLookout.com say 6 ft; a Willhite note puts the 1936 photo roof 15 ft above ground
facts.status_note: The cab was gone by 1952, per the register, FireLookout.com and the Willhite guide. No source describes a structure on the summit today.

access.note: Cross-country from the end of Forest Road 170 (a downed tree about a mile up the road), per a hiker's trip report. No closure appears in the sources read.

visit.trail_note: No maintained trail. A hiker's route runs up Forest Road 100 and FR-170, then cross-country up the southeast ridge. No tower remains to climb.

events.note: Wooden L-4 tower with a cab built, per the register, FireLookout.com and the Willhite guide
Panoramic photos taken July 25, 1936; the Willhite guide says they were taken on the roof, 15 feet above the ground
Cab gone by 1952; the sources do not say how

evidence.supports: Register places the site in the Okanogan National Forest
Built in 1935 as a 6-foot wooden L-4 tower; gone by 1952
evidence.quote: Built in 1935, this 6' wooden L-4 tower was gone by 1952.

evidence.supports: FireLookout.com: 6-foot wooden L-4 tower in 1935, gone 1952
Willhite: 6-foot wooden tower with an L-4 cab built in 1935
evidence.quote: In 1935 a 6 foot wooden tower with an L-4 cab was built.

evidence.supports: Willhite: 1936 panoramic photos taken on the roof, 15 feet above the ground
evidence.quote: In 1936 panoramic photos were taken on the roof at 15 feet above the ground.
By 1952 the lookout cab was gone.

evidence.supports: Route: drive up the West Chewuch to Forest Road 100
evidence.quote: I drove north out of Winthrop about 14.5 miles up the West Chewuch to Forest Road 100.

evidence.supports: Road FR-170 ends at a downed tree a little over a mile up
evidence.quote: A little over a mile after turning onto FR-170, there is a downed tree that signals the end of the road

evidence.supports: Cross-country route up the southeast ridge
evidence.quote: From here, I headed upslope to attain Doe's southeast ridge.

evidence.supports: Summit benchmarks and small remnants (melted lead glass, ceramic insulators, hinges, nails)
evidence.quote: I found the summit benchmarks as well as remnants of what looked to be melted lead glass, a few ceramic insulators, and some other small artifacts like hinges and nails.

evidence.supports: Cross-country route: the trip was a cross country peakbagging mission
evidence.quote: a spectacular cross country peakbagging mission to the summits of Doe Mountain

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register and FireLookout.com give the tower as 6 feet. The Willhite guide's note on the 1936 photos puts the roof 15 feet above the ground. The sources were not reconciled, so the story reports both and no height_m is recorded.

notes_for_editor: The history rests on three sources that agree on 1935 and gone-by-1952, and on the register and Weebly panorama dates. Today's site rests on one personal trip report, which gives no date for the visit. No staffing names appear in any source read, so the story says nothing about staffing. The 6-foot versus 15-foot height conflict is left open. The register says Okanogan National Forest; the Forest Service alerts page (search snippet only) uses Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, so check the current name before publishing. Access is inferred from the trip report and the TrailChick route; no source gives an official access status. Story is ~250 words.
